On a **V against I** graph the slope is the **resistance**, and a metal's resistance rises
with temperature.
**Step 1 — identify what the slope means.** From V = IR,
slope = V/I = **R** ✓
so the steeper line belongs to the larger resistance.
**Step 2 — read the graph.** The line labelled **T₁** is the **steeper** of the two, so
**R₁ > R₂** ✓
**Step 3 — connect resistance to temperature.** For a metallic conductor,
R_t = R₀(1 + αΔt), with α **positive** ✓
so a higher resistance means a **higher temperature**.
**Step 4 — conclude.**
**T₁ > T₂** ✓
**Why a metal's resistance rises with temperature.** Hotter lattice ions vibrate with
greater amplitude, so conduction electrons collide more often and the mean free time τ
falls ✓ Since
ρ = m/(ne²τ)
the resistivity rises. The number of carriers n hardly changes in a metal.
**The contrast with a semiconductor.** There, heating liberates many more carriers and
n rises steeply, so the resistance **falls** ✓ The same graph would then give T₁ < T₂ -
which is why the question specifies a conductor.
**Why the lines are straight.** Both obey **Ohm's law** at a fixed temperature ✓ A
curved V-I line would indicate non-ohmic behaviour, or that the conductor was heating up
as the current rose.
**A worked instance.** Copper has α ≈ 0·004 K⁻¹:
at 20 °C: R = 10 Ω
at 120 °C: R = 10(1 + 0·004 x 100) = **14 Ω** ✓ a 40% rise for a 100 K increase, easily
visible as a change of slope.
**How to read such a graph quickly.** Pick any convenient current and compare the two
voltages ✓ The line needing the **greater** voltage for that current has the greater
resistance, and hence the higher temperature.
**Reading the distractors.** **T₁ < T₂** ✗ reverses the relation between slope and
resistance. **T₁ = T₂** ✗ would need the two lines to coincide ✓
∴ T₁ > T₂.

Use U = ½CV², keeping careful track of the micro prefix.
**Step 1 — write the formula.**
U = ½CV² ✓
**Step 2 — substitute.**
U = ½(10 x 10⁻⁶)(10)²
= ½(10 x 10⁻⁶)(100)
**Step 3 — evaluate.**
= ½(10⁻³)
= 5 x 10⁻⁴ J
= **500 µJ** ✓
**Working in microjoules directly.** With C in µF and V in volts,
U(µJ) = ½ C(µF) V²
= ½(10)(100)
= **500 µJ** ✓ which avoids the powers of ten entirely and is the safer route under
exam conditions.
**The three equivalent forms.**
U = ½CV² = **Q²/2C** = **½QV** ✓
Here Q = CV = 10 µF x 10 V = **100 µC**, so
½QV = ½(100 x 10⁻⁶)(10) = **500 µJ** ✓ the same by a second route.
**Why the factor of ½.** The capacitor charges up **gradually**: the first charge
crosses at almost no voltage, the last at the full V ✓ The average is V/2, so
U = Q(V/2) = ½QV. Using QV without the half - the commonest error here - gives 1000 µJ,
which is exactly the second distractor.
**Where the energy is stored.** In the **electric field between the plates** ✓ with
energy density ½ε₀E² joules per cubic metre. Discharging the capacitor releases it as
heat, light or work.
**A sense of the quantity.** 500 µJ is half a millijoule - enough to lift a paperclip
about a centimetre ✓ Capacitors store modest energies but can release them extremely
quickly, which is what makes them useful in flash guns and defibrillators.
**Reading the distractors.** **1000 µJ** ✗ omits the ½. **100 µJ** ✗ is the **charge**
in µC read as an energy. **1 µJ** ✗ is a factor of 500 out ✓ Substituting into
½CV² checks any of them in one line.
∴ 500 μJ.

Heat produced at constant resistance goes as the **square of the voltage**, so the graph
is a rising parabola.
**Step 1 — write the heat developed in time t.**
U = Pt = (V²/R)t ✓
**Step 2 — see the dependence.** With R and t fixed,
**U ∝ V²** ✓
**Step 3 — identify the curve.** U against V is a **parabola through the origin**,
rising with ever-increasing steepness - concave **upwards** ✓ That is the third graph.
**Checking the key features.**
at V = 0: U = **0** ✓ the curve must pass through the origin, since no voltage means no
heating
the slope **increases** with V, since dU/dV = 2Vt/R grows ✓
doubling V **quadruples** U ✓
**A numerical illustration.** With R = 10 Ω and t = 1 s:
V = 1 V: U = **0·1 J**
V = 2 V: U = **0·4 J** - four times
V = 3 V: U = **0·9 J** - nine times ✓ the square law in plain numbers.
**Why the other curves fail.**
the **saturating** curve ✗ would mean the heating levels off at high voltage, which
nothing in P = V²/R allows
the **falling** curve ✗ has heat **decreasing** with voltage - the reverse of the
physics
the **straight line** ✗ would mean U ∝ V, which holds only if the **current** were
constant rather than the resistance ✓
**The three forms of Joule's law.**
U = I²Rt - use when the **current** is fixed
U = V²t/R - use when the **voltage** is fixed ✓
U = VIt - the general form
Choosing the right one depends on what is held constant; here it is the resistance and
the question varies V, so the middle form applies.
**The practical consequence.** A 10% rise in mains voltage raises a heater's output by
**21%** ✓ which is why appliance ratings specify the supply voltage so precisely.
**A caution for real conductors.** As the wire heats, R itself rises, so the curve is
slightly less steep than a pure parabola ✓ The question says "a given time" and treats
R as constant, which is the standard idealisation.
∴ the parabola rising from the origin.

For a long straight wire the field falls off as **1/r**.
**Step 1 — write the field.** From Ampere's law applied to a circle of radius r around
the wire,
B(2πr) = μ₀I
**B = μ₀I/(2πr)** ✓
so **B ∝ 1/r**.
**Step 2 — see why Ampere's law gives this at once.** By symmetry B is constant in
magnitude round the circle and tangential to it, so the line integral is simply B times
the circumference ✓ The enclosed current is I whatever the radius, so B must fall as
1/r to keep the product constant.
**A worked value.** For I = 10 A:
at r = 1 cm: B = (2 x 10⁻⁷)(10)/0·01 = **2 x 10⁻⁴ T**
at r = 2 cm: **1 x 10⁻⁴ T** ✓ exactly halved
at r = 10 cm: **2 x 10⁻⁵ T** ✓ a tenth
**The contrast with other geometries.**
**long straight wire**: B ∝ **1/r** ✓
**centre of a circular loop**: B = μ₀I/2R, with no distant field to speak of
**on the axis of a loop, far away**: B ∝ **1/r³** - the dipole law
**inside a long solenoid**: B = μ₀nI, **uniform** and independent of position ✓
Each geometry has its own dependence, and the 1/r law belongs specifically to the
infinite straight wire.
**Why not 1/r².** That is the **inverse-square** law of a **point** charge or mass ✓ A
wire is a one-dimensional source extending to infinity, and integrating the
Biot-Savart contributions along it turns the 1/r² of each element into an overall
1/r.
**The direction.** Circles around the wire, given by the **right-hand grip rule** ✓ The
magnitude falls as 1/r but the field never points away from the wire - it always
encircles it.
**Where the 1/r law is used.** In defining the **ampere** through the force between two
parallel wires, F/L = μ₀I₁I₂/(2πd) ✓ which follows directly from this field.
**Reading the distractors.** **1/r²** ✗ is the point-source law. **1/r³** ✗ is the
far-field dipole law. **1/√r** ✗ corresponds to no standard geometry ✓
∴ 1/r.
